attestations.notes: Proof 1.1–4.1 read: nonempty first-order domain supplies a set, Separation with z≠z gives existence, and Extensionality gives uniqueness. No choice axiom is used.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: x≠∅ licenses one member B, Separation bounds the universal membership class inside B, and Extensionality removes dependence on B. Empty indexing families are explicitly excluded.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: the weak Power Set axiom supplies a bounding set, Separation removes surplus elements, and Extensionality gives the exact unique power set, including x=∅.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: each union/intersection identity is checked by membership. Singleton and pair indexing sets are nonempty even when their members are empty or equal; no intersection of an empty family is claimed.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: a,b∈A∪B place {a} and {a,b} in its power set; their unordered pair is a subset of that power set. Equal coordinates and empty A/B cause no exception.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: substitution proves the reverse implication; the forward implication separates a=b and a≠b and exhausts the pair membership alternatives. The singleton specialization follows in both directions.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: applying the unordered-pair criterion to Kuratowski pairs yields two exhaustive alternatives, both forcing a=c,b=d, including all collapsed singleton cases. The converse is substitution.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: both coordinates of every Kuratowski pair in R lie in ⋃⋃R; two applications of Separation give domain and range without Replacement or choice. R=∅ is covered.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: Infinity bounds the class-wide intersection using Separation in I₀; zero and successor closure give inductivity, and mutual inclusion gives uniqueness. Quantification over inductive sets does not form a set of all such sets.

Proof 1.1–5.1 read: a subset containing zero and closed under successor is inductive, hence contains ω by minimality. Separation supplies the definable-property subset and proves equivalence with the set form.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction proves transitivity and self-irreflexivity together. In the successor case both possible self-membership routes force n∈n; Foundation is unnecessary.

Proof 1.1–6.1 read: intersecting the nonempty set of closed subsets of N×A gives a least closed relation. Removing an extra zero/successor value preserves closure using P1/P2; induction gives total functionality and uniqueness. a∈A excludes A=∅.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: successor contains n and is nonzero; equal successors with distinct coordinates force mutual membership and violate transitivity/irreflexivity. Induction is the already established principle.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: recursion with A=ℕ, initial value m and successor gives each unique s_m; its evaluation defines the total binary operation and the two equations. Uniform uniqueness requires no choice.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on c preserves arbitrary a,b; the zero case and recursive successor equations establish associativity without assuming commutativity.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on n establishes left identity from addition recursion; right identity is its defining zero equation. Base n=0 is explicit.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on the second argument establishes the first-argument successor law directly from recursion, with m fixed arbitrarily; no commutativity is assumed.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on n uses the proved left identity at zero and left-successor law at the induction step. Both summands remain arbitrary naturals.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on the common right summand has the hypothesis quantified over m,n; injectivity of successor reduces the successor case. Zero cancellation is explicit.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: the subset of naturals that are zero or successors contains zero and is successor closed; induction proves the dichotomy. The existential witness is the immediately preceding n.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: cancellation and nonzero-successor laws exclude simultaneous strict comparisons; induction with m universally quantified proves comparability. Positive additive increments cannot leave a natural unchanged.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: zero gives reflexivity, associativity composes order witnesses, trichotomy gives totality, and cancellation plus impossibility of a nonzero summand in a zero sum gives antisymmetry.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: nonzero additive increments are successors, so both directions convert between m<n and σ(m)≤n. Cancellation excludes equality in the reverse direction; linear-order incompatibility gives the no-intermediate-point conclusion.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: relation elements supply both coordinates for the product inclusion; the forward iff uses uniqueness of ordered-pair coordinates and the reverse uses coordinate membership. Empty relations are vacuous in both directions.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: inverse and composite pairs are bounded by range×domain and domain×range products before Separation; restriction is separated within R. Empty carriers and equal coordinates remain legitimate.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: zero differs from its successor by P1; successor injectivity transports the induction hypothesis. No membership order is assumed.

Proof 1.1–6.1 read: first establish ω transitive and the discrete successor-order law, then independently induct in both directions of membership/order. Subset/order reverse uses self-irreflexivity, avoiding ordinal circularity; zero is included.

Proof 1.1–7.1 read: a codomain transposition sends the top point to the top value, leaving an injection σ(n)→n after restriction and contradicting induction. Restrictions, inverse bijections and one explicit missing point give all four consequences; zero and equal transposition entries are covered, without AC.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: assuming a nonempty subset has no least member, zero is absent and the set of excluded initial intervals is successor closed. Discreteness and trichotomy justify the successor case; induction forces the subset empty.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: recursion with initial value zero and x↦x+m yields a unique total p_m, and evaluation supplies multiplication and its two recursive clauses. Every construction is determined, without choice.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: associativity/commutativity translate order witnesses across a common summand, and cancellation recovers the reverse witness. Equality reflection supplies both strict-order implications, including k=0.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: the right unit follows by one recursive step; simultaneous induction proves left zero and left unit using n+1=σ(n). Definitional right zero and n=0 agree.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on c proves left distributivity, while the explicitly written second induction on n proves the left-successor product rule. Only additive laws and multiplication recursion are used.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction on n uses left-zero at base and the independent left-successor product law at the step. No multiplicative commutativity is used before its conclusion.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: multiplication recursion reduces the successor case to left distributivity and the induction hypothesis; zero gives the base for arbitrary a,b.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: nonzero m,n are successors, and their product is explicitly a successor σ(mb+a), hence nonzero by P1. The contrapositive has exactly the claimed disjunctive conclusion.
Proof 1.1–2.1 read: a witness n=m+d gives nk=mk+dk. For strict order d,k are nonzero, so dk≠0, and additive cancellation excludes equality. k=0 is allowed only for the non-strict conclusion.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: two representative equivalences add and regroup into the required equivalence for addition; reversing coordinates gives negation equivalence. Degenerate zero representatives cause no exception.

Proof 1.1–5.1 read: expansions reduce one-factor replacement to a+b′=b+a′, symmetry gives replacement of the other factor, and transitivity combines them. All algebra takes place in ℕ before passage to classes.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: the quotient operations are first well-defined, then each ring law is checked on representatives. The two cubic expansions agree, distributivity is explicit, and swapping coordinates gives additive inverses.

Proof 1.1–5.1 read: translation invariance cancels the common summand to prove representative independence in both directions. Order laws follow from ℕ, and the positive-product gap is km with k,m≠0. Reflexivity follows directly from reflexivity of natural order.
Proof 1.1–4.1 read: distributivity gives 0a=0a+0a and additive cancellation gives 0a=0 for every a, including a=0. Commutative field addition licenses cancellation on the displayed side.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: differences of translated values equal b−a; the difference of sums is (b−a)+(d−c), positive by cone closure. No completeness or Archimedean assumption enters.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: three distributive identities yield zero sums, then additive inverse uniqueness proves one-negative and two-negative product identities. The previously read zero-product lemma supplies every zero product.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: cone multiplication and negative-product algebra prove all sign rules; each order-reflection direction explicitly excludes equality and opposite strict order by trichotomy. c=0 is excluded exactly where required.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: trichotomy splits nonzero a into positive and negative cases; cone closure and (−a)²=a² give strict positivity in both. The nonzero hypothesis excludes the zero-square endpoint.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: the field hypothesis gives 1≠0 and 1²=1, so the nonzero-square lemma yields 0<1. The trivial ring is explicitly excluded by the field axiom.

Proof 1.1–5.1 read: a positive element has nonzero inverse; a negative inverse would make aa⁻¹=1 negative. Multiplication by the positive a⁻¹b⁻¹ reverses the reciprocals under 0<a<b; neither zero denominator is allowed.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: evaluating two identities at each other proves uniqueness; associativity with two candidate inverses proves inverse uniqueness, repeated in F∖{0} multiplicatively. Inverse notation is restricted to nonzero x.
Proof 1.1–3.1 read: exhaustive nonzero sign cases make xy strictly positive or negative. Applying this zero-divisor exclusion to (x−y)z gives cancellation with precisely z≠0.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: cross-multiplication of the two representative equivalences proves product and sum equivalence, and multiplication by −1 gives negation. Every denominator is nonzero; products remain nonzero by the integer cancellation interface.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: representative expansions verify the ring laws; integer zero-divisor exclusion preserves denominators. Distributive representatives differ by the nonzero common factor b, and a≠0 licenses the inverse (b,a); 1≠0 is explicit.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: positive-denominator representatives allow order-preserving multiplication and cancellation in ℤ. Cross-product equivalences prove independence (the same symmetric argument gives the converse), and positive denominators give transitivity, addition compatibility and positive products.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: evaluating e*f with the left and right identity laws gives both f and e. Each uniqueness consequence specializes this equality; associativity is never used and identity existence is not claimed.

Proof 1.1–4.1 read: h=h*(g*h′)=(h*g)*h′=h′ uses associativity exactly once. Both one-sided inverses give invertibility; uniqueness of a one-sided inverse is asserted only when g already has a two-sided inverse.

Proof 1.1–3.1 read: induction from n=1 proves positivity, adding 1 gives successive strict increase, and finite iteration gives injectivity. Separate explicit inductions establish sum/product compatibility; the zero convention is consistent.

Proof 1.1–2.1 read: quotient equality identifies [(m,0)] injectively; the defining formulas preserve arithmetic and order. For [(a,b)]≥0, the natural gap a=b+k produces [(k,0)], and injectivity supplies its uniqueness.
